title: Inference Speed
text:
Inference Speed
Model inference is often measured relative to two phases
The first phase is prefill, or prompt processing, which occurs when your input tokens are processed
Typically measured in terms of time-to-first-token (TTFT) or prefill tokens-per-second (tok/s) at various prompt lengths
The second phase is decode, or token generation, which involves how quickly output tokens are generated
Typically measured in tokens-per-second (tok/s)
These metrics are generally not linear and vary based on factors such as context length

title: KV Caching
text:
KV Caching
A single LLM response can involve a sequence of many inference passes (e.g., once per every output token in the response)
By using a key-value (KV) cache, decoding can move faster by avoiding the need to reprocess prior tokens when generating new ones, reducing TTFT
The tradeoff of KV cache is increased memory demands

title: Prompt Caching
text:
Prompt Caching
Prompt (or prefix) caching extends this performance boost by allowing KV cache to be reused across requests
For example, consider a long agentic session involving a ten messages with 100K tokens in use. The user is about to send their eleventh message of 1K tokens:
Without prefix caching, the model must prefill the full 101K tokens before beginning generation
With prefix caching, the model can reuse the KV cache for the previous 100K tokens and process only the new 1K tokens, leading to significantly lower TTFT

title: Speculative Decoding
text:
Speculative Decoding
Speculative decoding is a method of “guessing” several upcoming candidate tokens (e.g., 3 tokens ahead) that are verified by the model in a single pass to improve throughput
Some methods under this umbrella such as multi-token prediction (MTP) are built into models (e.g., Qwen3.8)
Others such as DSpark, DFlash, and DFlash 2 involve a separate drafter model that works in conjunction with a larger model
Benchmarking speculative decoding at a variety of output (i.e., 3 vs. 5 tokens) and context lengths is important, as longer lengths can hinder speedup (also see Adaptive MTP)

title: Concurrency
text:
Concurrency
Concurrency involves processing multiple prompts/requests simultaneously to increase computational efficiency
Can be combined with continuous batching, where multiple requests are strategically combined into a single execution step, to further improve performance

title: Quantization
text:
Quantization
Quantization is a process for scaling and rounding model parameters to make models smaller and potentially faster
Many models are trained at 16-bit precision (e.g., FP16, BF16), but this can be reduced to 8-bits (e.g., FP8) or 4-bits (e.g., INT4) without significant accuracy degradation
For example, consider Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct
16-bits: ~61GB; 8-bits: ~31GB; 4-bits: ~17GB
Quantization can also be applied to model context (e.g., TurboQuant), although this can lead to output quality degradation (particularly below FP8) or a performance hit

title: Quantization Formats
text:
Quantization Formats
Various quantization formats exist to help reduce hardware requirements and improve inference performance
Use the ones appropriate to your hardware
Prefer 4-bit (or larger) formats
Popular options (mid 2026)
GPU: AWQ, GPTQ, NVFP4, FP8
Apple M chips: MLX, oQ+
CPU+GPU (includes Apple M chips): GGUF (e.g., Q4_K_M for 4-bits)

title: Model Types: Instruct, MoE
text:
Model Types: Instruct, MoE
Instruct (Instruction Tuned)
Tunes a base model to take an instruction and provide one response
Not necessarily tuned for multi-turn “chat”
MoE (Mixture of Experts)
Model consists of several mini-models or “experts”
Only some “active” experts will respond to a particular input
Performance can be significantly faster (in tokens/sec) than a “dense” model (i.e., non-MoE)

title: Other Model Considerations

Other Model Considerations
Multimodal
Some models work with modalities beyond text, e.g., vision, audio
These vision-language models (VLMs) may include “VL” or “V” in the model’s name
Thinking/Reasoning
Some models simulate cognitive processing (e.g., chain-of-thought [CoT]) for internal planning, often allowing for better response quality
Tool Calling/Tool Use/Agentic
Some models advertise “agentic” abilities, which include setting goals, planning, and acting while using “tools” to complete tasks

Cons: slower; require more hardware for local deployment; more expensive in the cloud
Additional considerations…
MoE models are often faster than dense models

Not all models accept multimodal inputs, optimize for tool usage, etc.

title: Context, Context, Context…
text:
Context, Context, Context…
Besides “intelligence,” one must consider context, or how much text (or other information) a model can access while generating subsequent tokens
Provides “working memory,” i.e., how much the model can remember and work with before forgetting
Measured in tokens (i.e., text chunks) and referred to as context length or context window
Covers both input and output tokens
TLDR: more context = better (especially for coding)

Context must be compressed, compacted, summarized, and/or pruned over time

Why This Matters…
Prompting goes beyond simply sending messages
Knowing more about how Hermes Agent processes your prompts provides insight into what you can control, allowing for changes in response quality
For example, as a user, you can alter Hermes’ system prompt—including its tone, personality, communication style, etc.—by editing your SOUL.md file

title: Conclusion
text:
Conclusion
Despite all the complexity, most aspects of prompt processing can be left to Hermes Agent and/or other tools to handle for you invisibly
The single most important thing you can do when prompting – be that sending messages to Hermes or to a model directly via an API request – is to tailor the user prompt to your task, which we cover in the next section

title: Same Prompt…Different Output
text:
Same Prompt…Different Output
The same prompt can produce a different output for a variety of reasons, including differences in:
Models (e.g., ChatGPT 5.6 Sol vs. Luna)
Reasoning effort (e.g., None vs. High)
Sampling parameters (e.g., temperature, top-p, top-k, seed)
System instructions
Conversation history and other context (e.g., tool results)
Chat templates and/or prompt formatting
Serving implementation, model quantization, hardware, etc.

title: Your Role
text:
Your Role
Despite these limitations, how you define and structure your prompt is the most critical aspect of maximizing output quality for a task
A poorly-written prompt can make a strong model underperform
A well-written prompt can make a weak model overperform (within the limits of model knowledge/capabilities)
This section focuses on the anatomy of a good prompt

Markdown

title: Example
text:
Example
You are an academic expert. Please follow all the instructions very carefully.
### Consider the following definition of banter:
- Banter is any teasing that runs along a continuum of bonding to biting.
- The banter must be in the dialogue (or a vocalization), not the prose.
- Humorous non-utterances do not count as banter.
### Task Overview
You will be given a dialogue pair and asked to determine if banter is present or not. The banter may be present in either or both parts of the dialogue pair, if present at all.
### You will make a determination if banter is present or not using this response scale:
0. Banter is not present
1. Banter is present
### Dialogue Pair
# Part A:
<inserted by script>
# Part B:
<inserted by script>
### Your Task
Answer the following question immediately by stating one response from the scale above verbatim.
YOUR RESPONSE MUST MATCH THE SCALE EXACTLY WITHOUT ALTERATIONS, INCLUDING THE SCALE RESPONSE NUMBER.
Does the dialogue pair contain banter?
Source: Dobolyi, K., Tamburrino, S., Borden, Z., & Faruque (2026, pgs. 58-59)
1. Define role: Explain to the AI agent who it is
2. Provide background: Inform AI agent of context
3. Define objectives: Explain to the AI agent your goals
4. Set parameters: Allow or limit tolerances
5. Be precise: Ensure your instruction or question is concise and explicit
6. Specify format: Describe or even provide a template

Prompting for Basic Tasks
Tasks such as the classification example on the previous slide require clarity and precision
Prompting the model repeatedly on a single piece of data can produce higher quality results than asking several questions at once
Try using different “shotting” techniques to improve results:
Zero-shot provides no examples when asking for a response
One-shot and few-shot offer one or many examples, respectively
Also consider positive vs. negative examples and contrastive prompting (Gao & Das 2024)

title: Prompting Complex Tasks (e.g., Coding)
text:
Prompting Complex Tasks (e.g., Coding)
Successfully accomplishing a complex task like coding requires step-by-step instruction (e.g., numbered lists)
Steps should be sequential
While multiple aspects can be worked in a single prompt, they may interfere with each other if they are not independent
A single, giant prompt can lead to missed or skipped steps
Be precise and do your research beforehand, e.g.,
What language do you want to code in?
What packages do you want to use?

title: Planning and Goals
text:
Planning and Goals
Working with a model to develop a plan (e.g., plan first…no code yet; “talk only”) or to establish goals can help by:
Breaking down a complex task into smaller steps (e.g., subgoals)
Providing a contract for you to analyze what the model did – and didn’t – do after the fact
Allowing for easier tracking of what’s already been done, which also helps understand what comes next
Plans/goals should include things that need to be done and things that shouldn’t be done (i.e., constraints)
Hermes (with a good model) may even ask you to clarify

title: Auditing, Verification, and GitHub
text:
Auditing, Verification, and GitHub
Never trust anything your agent does
You must review, audit, check, verify
Ask your model to summarize everything it did in the last turn(s) and commit this record to GitHub
Maintaining code on GitHub helps provide context for future work as well as recovery from mistakes/problems (e.g., by reverting commits)
Sources: Acuna, K. (2015, March 31); Nolan, C. (2014)

Hermes Agent Commands
Beyond just typing prompts, Hermes provides several commands to help manage more complex tasks, including:
/prompt – Compose your next prompt in $EDITOR (markdown), then send it (aka /compose)
/queue – Queue a prompt for the next turn (doesn’t interrupt)
/steer – Inject a message after the next tool call without interrupting
/goal – Set a standing goal Hermes works on until achieved
/subgoal – Add or manage extra criteria on the active goal
/plan – Write a markdown implementation plan…without executing anything
/kanban – Multi-profile collaboration board (tasks, links, comments)

What Is RAG?
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) retrieves relevant information from documents, databases, and other data sources and adds it to a model’s context to help generate a response to a user’s prompt/question

Why Use RAG?
RAG gives a model access to information beyond its training data, including more recent or private information
It selects relevant material from a large collection – or corpus – and grounds responses in sources, making answers easier to verify, potentially reducing hallucinations

title: Semantic Search and Embeddings
text:
Semantic Search and Embeddings
RAG often uses semantic search, or search based on meaning, to retrieve info relevant to the user’s question
Semantic search typically uses embeddings to numerically represent text, images, and other data
Embeddings are like coordinatesin high-dimensional space: similar items tend to lie closer together
Vector search compares the question’s embedding with data embeddings to find potential matches

doc: Week 5 - Context Engineering and RAG v1.pptx
title: Preparing Documents (Docs) for Search
text:
Preparing Documents (Docs) for Search
Docs added or updated in the RAG corpus must be prepared for search
Parsing extracts text and structure from each doc
Chunking divides the parsed content of each doc into useful passages while preserving source metadata (e.g., doc name, page number)
Indexing prepares the chunked passages for both:
Keyword (lexical) search to find chunks containing matching words
Vector search, which uses embeddings to find chunks with similar meanings

doc: Week 5 - Context Engineering and RAG v1.pptx
title: Each chunk should contain just enough context to be useful in isolation
text:
Each chunk should contain just enough context to be useful in isolation
Common chunking strategies:
Fixed size – chunks with a set size, often with overlap
Recursive – split at boundaries like paragraphs, then divide oversized chunks at finer boundaries like sentences
Document-based – keep related information together based on structural boundaries such as headings (see example above)
Semantic – split based on changing topics or meanings
Chunking: How Much Context Is Enough?

Hybrid RAG Pipeline with Reranking
RAG uses information from prepared documents to help an LLM answer the user’s question
Retrieval finds relevant candidate chunks using both keyword search and vector search in Hybrid RAG
Reranking compares these candidates to the original question and prioritizes which chunks are supplied to the LLM as context

title: What Goes In vs. What Comes Out
text:
What Goes In vs. What Comes Out
A modality is a type of content, e.g., text, image, audio, and/or video
A multimodal model works with multiple modalities across inputs, outputs, or both
A vision-language model (VLM) works with both visual content and language (e.g., describe this picture)
A multimodal large language model (MLLM) is a broader term for an LLM that works beyond text (i.e., many modern VLMs are also MLLMs)
Different models support different input → output combinations
Visual understanding: receipt image + “The total?” → text answer
Transcription: speech recording → text transcript
Image generation: text description → generated image

title: Multimodal != Generative
text:
Multimodal != Generative
Generative models produce content, including transcriptions, answers, or novel media
A model can be multimodal without being generative
Consider models we used for RAG:
Multimodal embedding and reranking models find relevant material via scoring and matching – but they do not generate content
VLMs (e.g., Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) generate answers based on retrieved visual information
Document VLMs such as dots.mocr generate text and layout information from page images, including optical character recognition (OCR) to recognize text in images

MBAX 6418 — Assignment 1: Sentiment & Emotion
Classification of Amazon Reviews
Goal: Produce a working review-sentiment classifier for Amazon reviews — it classifies each
review as positive / neutral / negative, detects the primary emotion, checks its predictions
against the star rating, and presents everything in a polished dashboard.
How to work on this: drive it with an agent — each step is a goal to reach, not a checklist. You
and the agent choose the approach as you go: API, tooling, structure, dashboard design. A few
fixed choices: the classification and scoring code is written in Python, and model calls go
through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint (e.g., the endpoints provided to the class). The
dashboard itself can be HTML or anything else. Work in order — each step should leave you
with something working. Your classmates are fair game for comparing approaches, asking
questions, and teaming up — but the write-up is owned by whoever submits it, and everyone
submits their own copy (see the GitHub section for how that works).
A note: where an earlier step hints at a later "known finding," treat it as a hunch to test — it's
more interesting if your numbers disagree.
(Useful if you haven't seen them: OpenAI offers verified US/Canada students $100 in ChatGPT
credits for use in Codex — https://developers.openai.com/community/students.)
The data
The task uses the Amazon 2023 "Gift Cards" review category — part of the large-scale
Amazon Reviews '23 dataset collected by the McAuley Lab at UC San Diego. You can learn
more about the dataset (its scale, other categories, and the full field reference) on the dataset's
site:
https://amazon-reviews-2023.github.io
The Gift Cards review file itself lives on the McAuley Lab's public dataset host:
https://mcauleylab.ucsd.edu/public_datasets/data/amazon_2023/raw/review_cate
gories/Gift_Cards.jsonl.gz
It is a gzipped JSON Lines (newline-delimited JSON) file; each line is one review. Expected
fields:

title: Page 2
text:
rating — the star rating, a number in {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} (encoded as a float, e.g., 4.0 ;
integral values throughout this dataset).
title — the short review-issue title.
text — the review body.
verified_purchase — boolean, whether the reviewer actually bought the item.
helpful_vote — integer count of "helpful" votes for the review.
timestamp — Unix milliseconds when the review was written.
images — array; image references attached to the review (often empty).
asin — the product this review is about.
parent_asin — the product family / parent item.
user_id — the reviewer.
Use your judgment about metadata worth keeping. Before building anything, confirm you can
actually read the file.
Step 1 — A structured prompt
A reusable prompt that takes a review's title and text and asks an LLM (see recommended
endpoint below) to classify it as POSITIVE or NEGATIVE. Decide the edge cases yourself
(conflicting title/text, terse or angry short reviews); the prompt must be set up so the model
gives you a clear, simple answer you can read back programmatically, and it must not rely on
the rating.
Ask yourself: does a quick spot-check on obviously positive and negative reviews come out
right?
Recommended LLM endpoint:
Base URL: http://dobolyi.com:9001/v1
API Key: 6418
Model Name: cyankiwi/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-AWQ-4bit
Step 2 — Score against the rating
Score a 100-row first batch and see how the model does against the "correct answer" you work
out from the rating (≥4 positive, else negative). The model must never see the rating — it's
only for checking afterwards. How you structure and save the work is up to you; at minimum, be
able to say how often the model agrees with the rating, which reviews it gets wrong, and a feel
for how often it's right on each class.

title: Page 3
text:
Ask yourself: can you say, with evidence, what the model is good and bad at? Keep in mind
the data is heavily skewed toward high ratings — most reviews are ★★★★ or ★★★★★ —
and don't let that lopsidedness fool you into thinking the model is better than it is.
Step 3 — A results dashboard
Present the results in a visual dashboard. A single self-contained HTML page is a good
option — everything baked into one file, works offline, no server or network needed — but
you're not limited to it: interactive app frameworks like Streamlit and Gradio work just as well.
Decide what belongs in it; at minimum the headline numbers, a clear picture of which answers
were right and wrong and how mistakes cluster by class, and enough per-review detail to back
up what you claim.
Design bar: this is a product, not a demo. Deliberate palette, refined typography, a coherent
theme the host can recolor — no library-shuffle look.
Ask yourself: do the numbers on the page match what your scoring produced, and can a non-
technical reader tell at a glance how good the model is?
Step 4 — Interactive review filtering
Make the review table explorable: let a reader filter to a subset (e.g., correct vs mismatched)
with a live count. Whether you do more than that is up to you.
Ask yourself: does filtering show exactly the rows you asked for, and does the count make
sense with what you recorded?
Step 5 — Primary-emotion detection
Add two independent takes on the review's primary emotion:
1. The LLM predicts it — extend the prompt's output so each review gives both sentiment
and a primary emotion.
2. A word list derives it — score each review's words against an NRC emotion word list (a
public list linking words to emotions: anger, anticipation, disgust, fear, joy, sadness, surprise,
trust), add the scores per emotion, and take the highest as the answer. This needs no
model calls and runs over your existing predictions.

title: Page 4
text:
Keep both, and compare them.
Ask yourself: how often do the two agree, and where/why do they diverge?
Step 6 — Three-class scoring with balanced sampling
Redefine to the full split:
Rating Class
4–5 POSITIVE
3 NEUTRAL
1–2 NEGATIVE
Carry the change through everything — the correct answer you work out, the numbers you
track, the prompt, and how the dashboard shows it. Because reading the first N rows in order
under-represents the rarer classes, instead pull a balanced group from the whole file — a
roughly equal number from each class, picked with a fixed random seed so the same set
comes up every time — around 50 per class.
Ask yourself: what do the balanced three-class numbers actually show, and what did the
balanced run reveal that the imbalanced one hid? In particular, do ★★★ (3-star) reviews get
their own class, or do they collapse into another?
Step 7 — Descriptive and prediction visualizations
Give the dashboard a descriptive layer — e.g., a star-rating distribution, a comparison of the
"correct answer" versus what the model predicted for each class, and how often each class was
answered right. The point is to make the model's failures visible at a glance.
Two things to be careful about:
Check the numbers on the page against the numbers you saved earlier — in the browser,
not just by eye.
Watch out for layout bugs that can collapse very small chart elements (e.g., bars given zero
width by a label/positioning interaction).
Ask yourself: can a reader see, without drilling in, where the model succeeds and fails?

title: Page 5
text:
Final deliverables
Produce a short report plus the working files: the prompt, the scoring script that runs the
reviews, the word-list script that adds the emotions, the dashboard generator, one balanced
run's raw output, and the final dashboard.
Report format: write it as markdown in a README.md (so it can later drop into a GitHub
repository as-is), and include one or more screenshots of at least the interface (for example,
a capture of the dashboard you built). Make sure every number you quote in it matches a visible
figure in the saved output. Also cite the source of the data (the Amazon Reviews '23 dataset
and its page) inside the README — don't expect a reader to go hunting for where the reviews
came from.
The report should be able to answer, with evidence:
1. Why did the lopsided run look very accurate, and what did sampling equal amounts of each
class change?
2. Look at where the model's mistakes go — which classes get confused with which, and in
what direction? (For example, do ★★★ (i.e., 3-star neutral) reviews get labeled negative,
or do negative ones get called neutral?) Report the concrete numbers from your matrix.
3. How do the LLM's emotions and the word list's emotions differ, and why?
4. What bugs and/or issues did you hit along the way — in the charts, the UI, in the process of
working with the agent, or anywhere else — and how did you work around them?
Author / review split: the report should be generated with the agent (it produces the draft,
pulls the numbers from the saved output, writes the narrative), but it is your deliverable —
review and check it yourself before submitting. Checking the claimed numbers against the
saved output and putting the agent's framing and conclusions into your own words is part of the
assignment, not an optional pass.
Submission: publish to GitHub and share the link
Requirement: the final README.md report and all the project code must live in a GitHub
repository, and you must hand in a shareable link to it. There is no alternative submission
path — the repo is the submission.
One per person, even in a team. If you work with classmates on the same work, you don't all
share one repo and one hand-in — each of you submits your own repository, even if it
contains essentially the same project. That requirement is there on purpose: it verifies that

GitHub access works for every person in the class, not just one or two per group. If a teammate
pushes and everyone else just forwards the same link, only that teammate's account has
proven GitHub works.
Public or private? Public is the simplest default — anyone with the link can read it, no extra
steps. Private works too, but it costs you one small step: add me
( david.dobolyi@colorado.edu ) as a collaborator on the repo, otherwise I can't see the files
when I open it. Do that after you create the repo, before you hand in the link.
Where to submit the link. The repo link is handed in as the assignment submission on
Canvas — put the shareable GitHub link in the Canvas submission so it's tied to your account
there. Just make sure the link you paste works (see the check further down) before you hit
submit.
New to GitHub? That's expected and fine — you'll likely need to create an account. Sign up
here if you don't have one:
https://github.com/signup
Because you're all students, the GitHub Student Developer Pack gives you free access to
tools that normally cost money — including GitHub Pro, Copilot, and Codespaces credits —
plus bundled tutorials for getting started with git and open source:
https://education.github.com/pack
The agent can and should help with every step. It can't sign up for you (only you can), but it
can:
guide you through account creation and the one-time setup (creating a token /
authenticating git ),
initialize a repository in your project folder,
stage and commit your code and the report,
create the GitHub repository and push to it,
for a private repo, invite me ( david.dobolyi@colorado.edu ) as a collaborator,
tell you how to confirm it's accessible and grab the shareable link.
Before you push, be deliberate about what goes in: include the code and the README.md ; think
about whether the data file (which is large and re-downloadable) or any credentials/tokens
belong in the repo — generally they don't. Ask the agent if you're unsure what's safe to commit.
Ask yourself: does the link you submit open a repository that you can access, and would the
person grading it be able to too — a public repo readably, or a private one after you've invited

title: Page 7
text:
them? Can they see the README (screenshots and all), and is the code there enough to
reproduce your results?
Standing considerations
The rating is the correct answer: it's what you judge the model against, but the model
never sees it.
Make your results repeatable: any number you publish should come from a fixed choice
of which reviews were used (a fixed "seed") and fixed settings, so running it again gives the
same answer.
Show your work: every number you claim should match the saved output — don't publish
something you haven't re-checked.
Be honest about imbalance: say openly how unbalanced the data is; never let a run that's
mostly one easy class look like proof the model is great.
Product bar: the dashboard is a finished, cohesive product.

Course Description
In this course, students will learn how to leverage recent advancements in generative artificial
intelligence (GAI) to solve business problems. The course focuses on three key aspects of GAI for
business. First, students will learn how best to use open and closed large language models (LLMs) for
coding, including topics such as AI-assisted coding, vibe coding, and debugging. Next, students will
develop their skills with models that focus on text as well as multimodal models incorporating text,
vision, and/or audio (e.g., text to image models): Relevant topics include fine-tuning, sustainable model
deployment, and agentic workflows. Finally, students will learn how to quickly and easily share their
models with stakeholders through a variety of methods and platforms, including graphical user
interfaces (GUIs), application programming interfaces (APIs), and local/cloud hosting options. Coding
experience is not a prerequisite for this course.
Course Objectives
• Survey the current state-of-the-art (SOTA) in open and closed GAI and LLMs
• Explore use cases for various model types, e.g., code-focused, multimodal, and reasoning models
• Become familiar with key GAI concepts such as model context protocol (MCP)
• Learn how to use AI coding agents effectively
• Fine-tune models to develop bespoke solutions to business challenges
